C005.object: in that they frame structural luck as a personal obstacle to be overcome rather than as a determining factor

[PATH:empirical] Comparative content analysis of motivational speeches, self-help literature, and biographical accounts from OECD countries (e.g., US, UK, Germany) vs. low-income economies (e.g., Sub-Saharan African nations) using a coding scheme for attributions of success (e.g., internal vs. external factors, framing of luck). — Directly tests the hypothesis by quantifying how structural luck is depicted as an obstacle versus a determining factor across GDP contexts, leveraging publicly available media and discourse data from 2000–2020.

[PATH:empirical] Survey experiments measuring perceptions of success narratives: present participants from high- and low-GDP countries with vignettes varying the framing of structural luck (obstacle vs. determinant) and assess their endorsement of personal agency vs. systemic barriers. — Provides causal evidence on how narrative framing influences beliefs about success, isolating the effect of GDP context via cross-national comparison and controlling for confounds like education or media exposure.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review of sociological and psychological literature on meritocracy beliefs and attribution theory (e.g., work by Kluegel & Smith, or Jost et al.) focusing on cross-national differences in how luck is conceptualized in success stories. — Synthesizes existing theoretical frameworks and empirical findings to contextualize the hypothesis, identifying gaps in current research that the hypothesis addresses, such as the role of economic development in shaping narrative conventions.

qualifier.geographic: OECD countries vs. low-income economies (World Bank classification)

[PATH:empirical] Cross-national content analysis of success narratives in mass media (e.g., newspapers, TV profiles) from selected low-GDP (e.g., Kenya, Bangladesh) and high-GDP (e.g., Germany, Canada) countries, coding for attributions to individual effort vs. structural factors. — Directly tests the hypothesis by comparing the prevalence of individual agency versus structural luck in public discourse across the specified geographic and temporal scope.

[PATH:empirical] Ethnographic interviews or survey experiments with individuals in low-GDP countries (Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia) eliciting personal success stories and probing perceived causes, contrasted with similar data from high-GDP Western countries. — Provides ground-level evidence of how people construct success narratives, revealing whether cultural emphasis on agency differs as hypothesized, and can capture nuance not available in media content alone.

[PATH:theoretical] Review of sociological and psychological literature on attribution theory, cultural models of achievement, and the 'American Dream' versus 'lottery/patronage' narratives in low-income contexts. — Establishes theoretical foundations and existing findings on how economic context shapes attribution patterns, helping to interpret empirical results and assess the plausibility of the hypothesis.

qualifier.geographic: low-GDP countries in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia vs. high-GDP countries in Western Europe and North America

C007.object: any acknowledgment of structural luck when success is inherited or elite, but reframe such luck as 'earned' through social or familial discipline
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: narratives of personal success in high-GDP countries any acknowledgment of structural luck when success is inherited or elite, but reframe such luck as 'earned' through social or familial discipline]

[PATH:empirical] Qualitative analysis of elite autobiographies and interviews (e.g., from the Pew Research Center or the British Social Attitudes Survey) to identify patterns in how inherited wealth is framed as 'earned' through discipline or family values. — Directly tests the hypothesis by examining narrative content from the target population (upper-class individuals in high-GDP countries) for suppression of structural luck and reframing as earned.

[PATH:empirical] Comparative survey experiments on public perceptions of inherited vs. self-made wealth (e.g., using vignettes that vary descriptions of success origin and measuring attributions to luck vs. effort), replicable in the US, UK, and Western Europe. — Provides causal evidence on whether narratives that suppress structural luck and reframe it as discipline are actively produced and accepted, or merely assumed by the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical review of sociological literature on 'meritocratic ideology' and 'class reproduction' (e.g., works by Pierre Bourdieu, Richard Sennett, or Michael Sandel) applied to late 20th/early 21st century elite discourse. — Contextualizes the hypothesis within established frameworks of how elites legitimize privilege, offering conceptual tools to interpret empirical findings and identify counter-narratives.

qualifier.geographic: high-GDP countries, particularly the United States, United Kingdom, and Western Europe

[PATH:empirical] Comparative analysis of national survey data (e.g., World Values Survey, ISSP) on beliefs about success attributions (hard work vs. luck/connections) among different socioeconomic groups in high-GDP countries. — Provides population-level evidence on whether the 'individual merit' narrative dominates even among upper-class respondents, complementing the content analysis.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical literature on 'meritocracy myth' and 'legitimating ideologies' (e.g., works by Michael Sandel, Paul Piff, or Daron Acemoglu) that examine how structural advantages are downplayed in self-narratives of the wealthy. — Offers a conceptual framework to interpret empirical findings and to predict conditions under which the hypothesis might hold or fail.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal survey data on locus of control and perceived causes of success from Afrobarometer or World Values Survey, stratified by age cohort (pre-1980 vs. post-1980) in Sub-Saharan African and South Asian low-GDP countries — Directly measures attribution of outcomes to luck/external circumstances vs. effort/skill across generations, allowing confirmation or refutation of the age-cohort claim in the specified geographic scope.

[PATH:empirical] Qualitative life-history interviews with older adults (born before 1980) in rural and urban communities in selected low-GDP countries in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, focusing on narratives of personal success and failure — Provides rich contextual data on how older generations construct causal explanations for outcomes, capturing cultural and experiential nuances that surveys may miss, and can test the hypothesis in community-oriented, low-mobility settings.

[PATH:literature] Comparative literature review of ethnographic studies on intergenerational mobility and success narratives in low-GDP countries, particularly works by Bourdieu, Rao, or recent development ethnographies — Synthesizes existing theoretical and empirical evidence on how structural constraints (e.g., low mobility, strong community ties) shape attributions of success, providing a foundation to assess whether the hypothesis aligns with established findings or reveals a gap.
